title: Can twice a sum of two squares be another sum of two squares?
description: The board shows twice the sum of five squared and six squared, and rewrites it as the squares of the sum and the take away of five and six. Adding the two expansions makes the middle terms cancel, which explains the pattern. Keeko doubts it and doubles both numbers instead, which gives four times the sum of squares.
teaching_notes: One idea: add the two numbers and take one from the other, then square both and add, to get twice the sum of the two squares. Watch for students who double both numbers, which makes four times the sum of squares.

source: Write 2 × (5² + 6²) as a sum of two squares, and explain why
video_script.why: The child has the expansions of a sum squared and a take away squared, but has not yet added them to see the pattern of twice the squares.
video_script.substitution: Use the sum and the take away of the two numbers as the new numbers, then add the two expansions so the middle terms cancel.
video_script.anchor: the book's pattern lines, two times a sum of two squares written as another sum of two squares
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko doubles both numbers, five and six, to ten and twelve, and adds their squares. That gives two hundred forty four, which is four times sixty one, not two times.
video_script.payoff_line: Two times, five squared plus six squared, is eleven squared plus one squared.
maths_rules: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²
(a + b)² + (a − b)² = a² + 2ab + b² + a² − 2ab + b² = 2a² + 2b² = 2(a² + b²)
pattern lines: 2 × (2² + 1²) = 3² + 1² since 2 + 1 = 3 and 2 − 1 = 1; 2 × (3² + 1²) = 4² + 2² since 3 + 1 = 4 and 3 − 1 = 2
video_script.design: One idea: the sum and the take away of the two numbers, squared and added, give twice the squares. The pattern lines stay on the board through the idea part. Keeko's wrong idea is to double both numbers.

narration: <bookmark mark='lines'/>Your book shows some lines of this pattern.
Two times, two squared plus one squared, is three squared plus one squared.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Here three is two plus one, and one is two minus one.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Two times, three squared plus one squared, is four squared plus two squared.
Here four is three plus one, and two is three minus one.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, two times, five squared plus six squared.

beats.on_screen: To find: write it as a sum of two squares, and say why

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to write it as a sum of two squares, and say why it works.
<bookmark mark='squares'/>Step one, find the value. Five squared is twenty five, and six squared is thirty six.
<bookmark mark='value'/>Their sum is sixty one, so two times sixty one is one hundred twenty two.

beats.on_screen: 6 + 5 = 11 and 6 − 5 = 1; 11² = 121 and 1² = 1; 121 + 1 = 122, the same value as step one

beats.colours: the sum in one colour, the take away in another
narration: <bookmark mark='pair'/>Step two, use the sum and the take away of the two numbers, as the pattern lines did.
<bookmark mark='pair2'/>Six plus five is eleven, and six minus five is one.
<bookmark mark='squares'/>Eleven squared is one hundred twenty one, and one squared is one.
<bookmark mark='match'/>One hundred twenty one plus one is one hundred twenty two, the same as step one.

beats.on_screen: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²; adding: 2ab and −2ab cancel, leaving 2a² + 2b² = 2(a² + b²)
beats.colours: the two middle terms in the accent colour
narration: <bookmark mark='plus'/>Step three, see why, by adding the two expansions. Eigh plus b all squared is eigh squared plus two eigh b plus b squared.
<bookmark mark='minus'/>Eigh minus b all squared is eigh squared minus two eigh b plus b squared.
<bookmark mark='cancel'/>Plus two eigh b and minus two eigh b cancel.
<bookmark mark='left'/>What is left is two eigh squared plus two b squared. That is two times eigh squared plus b squared.

marks.why: the reason is written under it

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Two times, five squared plus six squared, is eleven squared plus one squared.
<bookmark mark='why'/>It works for any two numbers, because the two eigh b terms cancel.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks twice the sum means doubling both numbers, so it is ten squared plus twelve squared.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Ten squared is one hundred, and twelve squared is one hundred forty four. Together they make two hundred forty four.
<bookmark mark='ratio'/>That is the same as four times sixty one.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>We need two times sixty one, not four times. Doubling both numbers makes each square four times bigger.
<bookmark mark='right'/>Only the sum and the take away of five and six give exactly twice.
